REDLINE ANALYSIS MEMORANDUM
Capital Markets — Counterparty Markup of Underwriting Agreement

PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL
Attorney Work Product / Prepared in Anticipation of Litigation

TO: Engagement File — Capital Markets
FROM: Capital Markets Deal Team
RE: Negotiation-Ready Redline Analysis of Underwriter's Markup to Underwriting Agreement
DATE: [Current Date]

I. INTRODUCTION AND SCOPE

This memorandum provides a negotiation-ready analysis of the underwriter's redline markup of the Underwriting Agreement against (i) our original draft and (ii) the firm's capital markets playbook and market practice. The counterparty's latest markup introduces a series of deviations across the operative provisions of the agreement — specifically the representations and warranties, covenants, conditions to closing, indemnification, and termination provisions. Each material deviation is analyzed below, with a recommended position (Accept, Reject, or Counter), supporting rationale grounded in market practice and firm precedent, and draft fallback language where necessary.

This memorandum is intended to equip counsel and the client for the forthcoming negotiation. Each flagged item is assigned a priority and roadmap for escalation. This document is privileged and prepared in anticipation of negotiation and potential litigation; it should not be shared with the counterparty.

II. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The underwriter's markup is aggressive in several respects and, if accepted in full, would materially shift risk allocation and economic exposure away from the underwriter and onto the issuer. The deviations fall into three categories:

• Category A — Market/Clean-Up/UNACCEPTABLE: Deviations that depart materially from market practice and firm precedent and should be rejected outright. These are concentrated in the indemnification and termination sections.
• Category B — Negotiable with Adjustments: Deviations that are acceptable in concept but require counter-language to moderate scope, allocate risk fairly, or conform to firm precedent. These are concentrated in the representations, warranties, and covenants sections.
• Category C — Acceptable/Conforming: Deviations that are immaterial, conforming, or market-consistent and may be accepted.

Of the counterparty's markups reviewed, approximately [X]% fall in Category A, [X]% in Category B, and [X]% in Category C. The overall portfolio position is that the issuer can accommodate a commercially reasonable markup while holding firm on the core risk-allocation and indemnification architecture described below.

III. ANALYSIS OF COUNTERPARTY MARKUP BY PROVISION

A. REPRESENTATIONS AND WARRANTIES

1. Issuer Representations & Warranties — Knowledge Qualifier Broadening
   Counterparty Markup: The underwriter seeks to broaden the knowledge qualifier on issuer representations and warranties from "Knowledge of the Company" to "Knowledge of the Company after due inquiry," and to extend the due-inquiry formulation to certain fundamental representations.
   Analysis: The proposed markup is inconsistent with the firm's capital markets playbook, which limits due-inquiry knowledge qualifiers to non-fundamental, non-speculative representations. Applying a due-inquiry qualifier to fundamental representations dilutes the issuer's core disclosure obligations and is non-market.
   Recommendation: REJECT the extension of the due-inquiry qualifier to fundamental representations. ACCEPT with limiting counter-language for non-fundamental representations. Proposed fallback: "Knowledge of the Company means the actual knowledge of the officers identified on Schedule [__] after reasonable inquiry of the individuals who supervise the relevant business functions."
   Priority: High.

2. Underwriter Representations & Warranties — Material Adverse Change Carve-Outs
   Counterparty Markup: The underwriter deleted the requirement that its representations and warranties survive beyond closing and added a broader "no breach" condition.
   Analysis: Survival of underwriter representations and warranties is a standard market term given the indemnity backstop. Deleting survival for the underwriter is non-market.
   Recommendation: REJECT the deletion of survival. ACCEPT in concept subject to restoring the market survival period. Prioritize restoration during negotiation of the indemnification section.
   Priority: High.

3. Financial Statement / Disclosure Representation — "No Omission" Standard
   Counterparty Markup: The underwriter seeks to change the issuer's disclosure representation from "no misstatement of a material fact or omission of a fact required to make the statements not misleading" to a stricter "no material omission of any fact, whether or not required to be stated."
   Analysis: The proposed alternative broadens the disclosure obligation to encompass facts not required to be stated, which is not the market standard under the Securities Act framework and would expose the issuer to unquantifiable liability.
   Recommendation: REJECT. The Securities Act standard already provides the appropriate disclosure baseline. No counter-language necessary beyond restoring the original formulation.
   Priority: Medium.

B. COVENANTS

4. Affirmative Covenant — Financial Statements and Reports Delivery
   Counterparty Markup: The underwriter added a covenant requiring delivery of unaudited monthly financial statements and a materially broader right to request additional information on demand during periods of market turbulence.
   Analysis: The firm's playbook permits quarterly (and, in some deals, semi-annual) reporting delivery, with a "commercially reasonable" information-request standard. Monthly unaudited delivery and an open-ended demand right are non-market and operationally burdensome.
   Recommendation: COUNTER. Replace "on demand during market turbulence" with "upon reasonable request" and extend delivery intervals to the market-standard quarterly cadence. Proposed fallback: "The Company shall furnish to the Representatives, as soon as reasonably practicable and in no event later than [__] days following the end of each fiscal quarter, the Company's quarterly financial statements."
   Priority: Medium.

5. Negative Covenant — Additional Financing Limitation
   Counterparty Markup: The underwriter seeks to restrict the issuer's ability to enter into specified substitute or additional financing arrangements without the underwriter's prior written consent.
   Analysis: A broad "prior written consent" over all additional financing is overly restrictive and inconsistent with common market terms, which generally restrict only financing that competes with or refinances the offering within a defined period.
   Recommendation: COUNTER. Limit the restriction to (i) a defined period post-closing and (ii) financing that would constitute a "change in control" trigger or compete with the offering. Proposed fallback: "The Company shall not, without the prior written consent of the Representatives, issue any securities that would be convertible into, or exchangeable for, Equity Securities in a manner that would result in a Change of Control during the Purchase Period."
   Priority: Medium.

6. Use of Proceeds Covenant — "Substantially In Accordance" Burden
   Counterparty Markup: The underwriter added language requiring the issuer to use net proceeds "substantially in accordance" with the use-of-proceeds description, but deleting the existing "in all material respects" qualifier and adding a certification requirement tied to each draw.
   Analysis: The "in all material respects" standard is market. The proposed per-draw certification is burdensome and invites breach claims on non-material deviations.
   Recommendation: COUNTER. Accept the "substantially in accordance" formulation if the materiality qualifier is retained; reject the per-draw certification. Proposed fallback: retain "in all material respects" and remove per-draw certification.
   Priority: Low.

C. CONDITIONS TO CLOSING

7. Bring-Down Certificate — Material Adverse Effect Standard
   Counterparty Markup: The underwriter deleted "material adverse effect" from the bring-down closing condition and replaced it with a broader, unqualified standard tied to the issuer's continuing ability to perform.
   Analysis: The "no material adverse effect" bring-down is a core market closing condition. Removing the MAE qualifier converts the closing condition into an unqualified ongoing-performance warranty and materially increases the issuer's pre-closing risk.
   Recommendation: REJECT removal of the MAE standard. Restore the market formulation. This is a Category A item.
   Priority: High.

8. Legal Opinion Condition — Expanded Opinion Scope
   Counterparty Markup: The underwriter added a condition requiring delivery of opinions covering "all matters that the Representatives reasonably consider necessary" and on the issuer's solvency and tax-substantiation matters.
   Analysis: Firm precedent standardizes the scope of legal opinions (validity, authorization, and enforceability, plus specified comfort). An open-ended "reasonably consider necessary" opinion requirement, plus solvency and tax-substantiation opinions, exceeds standard market scope and creates unreasonable delay risk.
   Recommendation: COUNTER. Set a definitive opinion scope schedule and expressly exclude solvency and tax-substantiation opinions unless otherwise agreed. Priority: High.

D. INDEMNIFICATION

9. Issuer Indemnification — Removal of the "In Proportion To" Loss Allocation / Broadening of Covered Claims
   Counterparty Markup: The underwriter revised the indemnification provision to (i) broaden covered claims beyond violations of the Securities Act and Exchange Act to include "any claim, loss, damage, or expense arising out of or relating to the offering or the performance of the Underwriting Agreement," and (ii) remove the contribution/"in proportion to" fault allocation, shifting the entire loss to the issuer.
   Analysis: This is the most significant deviation in the markup. Standard market indemnification is limited to securities-law violations and materially similar claims, with contribution allocated in proportion to relative fault and benefit. The counterparty's broadened "arising out of or relating to" language would convert the agreement into a blanket indemnity for the underwriters' own negligence and bad faith, which is flatly contrary to firm precedent and market practice.
   Recommendation: REJECT. This is a Category A item and a firm redline. Restore the standard carve-out for the underwriters' own negligence, willful misconduct, or breach, and restore proportional-fault contribution. Proposed fallback: "The Company shall not be liable under the indemnification provisions for any Losses to the extent finally judicially determined to have resulted primarily from or be directly attributable to the gross negligence, willful misconduct, or bad faith of the Representatives or from a breach of the Representatives' representations and warranties."
   Priority: Highest.

10. Earnings/Coverage Cap and Loss Definition
    Counterparty Markup: The underwriter removed the existing cap on indemnification exposure and broadened the definition of "Losses" to include indirect, consequential, and punitive damages and lost profits.
    Analysis: Market terms typically cap aggregate indemnification exposure and exclude consequential, punitive, and lost-profits damages absent willful misconduct. Removal of the cap and broadening of "Losses" is non-market.
    Recommendation: REJECT removal of the cap. COUNTER to define "Losses" to exclude indirect, special, consequential, punitive, and exemplary damages and lost profits, except where finally adjudicated to arise from fraud or willful misconduct. Priority: Highest.

E. TERMINATION

11. Termination for "Period of Market Disruption" — Broadened Definition
    Counterparty Markup: The underwriter redefined the traditional market-out provision (general moratorium, material adverse change, suspension of trading, outbreak of hostilities) to add an overbroad "period of market disruption" that would allow termination based on ordinary market volatility.
    Analysis: Market-out provisions are narrow and require a material disruption beyond ordinary volatility. Broadening to permit termination on any period of market disruption would give the underwriter a unilateral walk right on ordinary market moves.
    Recommendation: REJECT the overbroad definition. COUNTER to require a "material adverse change in the financial markets that, in the reasonable judgment of the Representatives, would make it impracticable or inadvisable to proceed with the offering," consistent with firm precedent. Priority: High.

12. Automatic Termination / Right to Cancel — Notice and Cure
    Counterparty Markup: The underwriter deleted the notice-and-cure mechanism in the termination provision.
    Analysis: Notice-and-cure is a standard market protection. Deleting it removes the issuer's ability to remedy a curable deficiency prior to termination.
    Recommendation: REJECT deletion. Restore a notice-and-cure mechanism with a defined cure period. Priority: Medium.

F. MISCELLANEOUS / OTHER DEVIATIONS

13. Governing Law and Forum
     Counterparty Markup: The underwriter retains market-standard governing law and forum, with no substantive deviation. ACCEPT.

14. Expense Reimbursement
     Counterparty Markup: The underwriter added a broader reimbursement of its expenses (counsel, experts, diligence) regardless of deal outcome.
     Analysis: Market terms typically cap expense reimbursement and tie reimbursement to a defined quantum. An uncapped, outcome-blind reimbursement is non-market.
     Recommendation: COUNTER to cap expense reimbursement at a set amount and limit to documented, reasonable out-of-pocket expenses. Priority: Low.

IV. NEGOTIATION ROADMAP AND PRIORITIES

Priority 1 (Hold-Firm / Category A): Items 9 and 10 (indemnification scope and Losses definition/cap), Item 7 (removal of MAE from bring-down), and Item 12 (notice-and-cure) are firm redlines. Counsel should hold firm and be prepared to walk rather than concede these core risk-allocation terms.

Priority 2 (Negotiate / Category B): Items 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 11, and 14 are negotiable with the counter-language set forth above. These items can be traded for Category A concessions.

Priority 3 (Accept / Category C): Item 13 and minor conforming edits, plus immaterial drafting clarifications, may be accepted to advance goodwill.

V. MARKET PRACTICE / REGULATORY FRAMEWORK NOTES

Underwriting agreements in equity and debt capital markets offerings are governed by the market-standard architecture reflected in the firm's playbook and in the applicable regulatory framework (including the Securities Act of 1933, the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, and FINRA Rule 5110 for certain underwritings). The core negotiating leverage in an underwriting agreement centers on (i) the scope of issuer representations and warranties, (ii) the conditions to closing (particularly the bring-down and legal opinion requirements), (iii) the indemnification and contribution framework, and (iv) the market-out/termination rights. The counterparty's markup targets precisely these leverage points, and the recommendations herein are calibrated to preserve the market-standard allocation of risk while allowing commercially reasonable concessions.

VI. CONCLUSION AND NEXT STEPS

The underwriter's markup, if accepted wholesale, would materially transfer risk to the issuer across the indemnification, termination, covenant, and closing-condition provisions. The issuer should enter the negotiation holding firm on the Category A items identified above and be prepared to make limited Category B concessions. Counsel should circulate this memorandum to the engagement team, incorporate the recommended counter-language into a clean redraft for the next round, and coordinate with the client on negotiation authority for the Priority 1 and Priority 2 items.

This memorandum is privileged and confidential, prepared in anticipation of negotiation and potential litigation, and constitutes attorney work product. Do not distribute outside the engagement team.

[End of Memorandum]
